extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of constitutional law, political theory, and comparative government
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of the principles, organization, jurisdiction, and procedural practices of the United States federal judiciary within a federal constitution. Focuses on why a separate federal judiciary is necessary, what cases it should hear, how it should be organized, and the political consequences of its powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a separate federal judiciary
rubrics_metrics.description: The Union could not adapt the judicial power of the States to its wants; to entrust the execution of the laws of the Union to tribunals instituted by these political bodies would be to allow foreign (partial) judges to preside over the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States form 'divers political bodies' with distinct origins and maxims; allowing state tribunals to enforce federal laws would give provincial and partial judges authority over national matters and risk inconsistent enforcement and partiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of federal jurisprudence
rubrics_metrics.description: To suppose that a State can subsist when its fundamental laws may be subjected to four-and-twenty different interpretations at the same time is contrary to reason and experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiplicity of state tribunals and divergent interpretations make state courts unfit to secure the uniform application of national law; centralizing interpretation in federal tribunals is necessary to maintain consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization of the federal judiciary (Supreme, Circuit, District)
rubrics_metrics.description: The entire judicial power of the Union was centred in one tribunal, the Supreme Court, with inferior courts appended (District Courts and Circuit Courts) to facilitate expedition of business; District judges preside locally, Circuit Courts try important causes, Supreme Court handles most serious cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inferior courts decide minor causes without appeal and larger causes with appeal; Supreme Court holds a yearly solemn session; jury was introduced in federal courts similar to state courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment, tenure, and salary protections for federal judges
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the Supreme Court are named by the President with the advice of the Senate; their office was made inalienable, and their salary, once fixed, should not be altered by the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisions were adopted to render federal judges independent of other authorities and to protect judicial impartiality from legislative or popular pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court decides both facts and law
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike the French Cour de Cassation, the Supreme Court decides upon the evidence of fact as well as upon the law of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court issues its own decisions (not merely remanding on legal questions), giving it a broader remedial and fact-finding role than purely appellate institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court's authority to determine questions of jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: It was necessary to allow one tribunal to judge its own cause; the Supreme Court of the United States was therefore invested with the right of determining all questions of jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granting this right to state courts would subvert federal sovereignty; centralizing jurisdictional determinations in the Supreme Court prevents conflicting claims of competency and ensures a uniform body of jurisprudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal jurisdiction defined by the parties involved and the nature of the cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain parties (e.g., ambassadors, the Union itself, parties from different States) and certain causes (e.g., maritime commerce, cases arising under US laws) must always be brought before Federal courts regardless of other circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinctions by party and subject matter form the basis of federal jurisdiction: the personal quality of litigants and the intrinsic nature of causes both prescribe competency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambassadors, the Union, and inter-state party suits belong in federal courts
rubrics_metrics.description: When an ambassador is a party or the Union itself is invoked in legal proceedings, those suits concern the whole Union and must be heard by Federal tribunals; similarly, when parties belong to different States, the Union's courts are the proper forum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories protect national interests (diplomatic relations, national sovereignty) and avoid bias that could arise if state tribunals tried such matters; includes state-versus-state litigation as uniquely national.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maritime, admiralty, and law-of-nations cases under federal jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: All questions concerning maritime commerce and matters connected with the interpretation of the law of nations fall under Federal tribunals, since the sea lies outside peculiar state jurisdiction and implicates national relations with foreign powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include piracy and other maritime offenses; maritime jurisdiction is inherently national and thus centralized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cases arising under the laws and treaties of the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: The judicial power of the Supreme Court shall extend to all cases in law and equity arising under the laws of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When state acts or disputes require interpretation of federal statutes or treaties (e.g., state laws on currency or import duties that conflict with federal law), federal courts must decide to protect federal supremacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal protection of contractual obligations against state laws (Contracts Clause)
rubrics_metrics.description: States are prohibited from passing laws impairing the obligations of contracts; if a state law does so, affected citizens may appeal to Federal courts (Dartmouth College example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracts granted by state charters are treated as contracts within the meaning of the Constitution; state laws that change such charters or private contractual rights can be declared void by federal tribunals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal jurisdiction extends to state laws that violate the Constitution (e.g., ex post facto)
rubrics_metrics.description: The jurisdiction of the Federal courts extends not only to cases arising under US laws, but also to those arising under laws made by the several States in opposition to the Constitution (e.g., ex post facto criminal laws).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citizens injured by enforcement of unconstitutional state laws can seek relief in federal courts; federal jurisdiction thus functions to restrain state encroachments on constitutional limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural strategy: bring private individuals before federal courts to attack state laws indirectly
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislators should strive to bring private individuals, and not States, before the Federal Courts; the Union tends to use private plaintiffs to contest state laws' consequences rather than suing States directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This indirect approach avoids placing the judicial power in direct hostility with States; federal courts then annul the effects of state laws by adjudicating private rights affected by those laws (less confrontational remedy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal judges should exercise prudence and respect public opinion limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Their power is enormous but is clothed in the authority of public opinion; they are the guardians of the Union but would be impotent against popular neglect or contempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal judges are conscious of the relative weakness of federal power and may be inclined to abstain from asserting jurisdiction in borderline cases to avoid political backlash or destabilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities required in federal judges: jurists must also be statesmen
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal judges must be good citizens with information and integrity, but they must also be statesmen—not afraid to brave obstacles or slow to tolerate encroachments that threaten the supremacy of the Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the Supreme Court influences the peace and existence of the Union, judges require political prudence and courage in addition to legal competence; imprudent or unworthy judges risk national instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political importance and preponderance of the Supreme Court
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court's prerogatives are almost entirely political; it enforces the laws of the Union and summons sovereign powers to its bar, rendering it a tribunal of the nation with responsibilities beyond private litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court's decisions affect relations among branches and between States and the Union; its centrality means its composition and conduct have wide political consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional design features that make the Federal Constitution superior to State constitutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Constitution is superior due to the wisdom of its framers: the national legislature and executive are less dependent on the people, the judiciary less subjected to majority inclinations, and terms and modes of election were adjusted to increase discretion and stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include longer terms for representatives, differing conditions of eligibility and modes of election for the two houses to temper popular passions, and selection mechanisms designed to foster independence and prudence.
